$comment: The pinned Covenant benchmark workload. Every number the release gate reports was produced against exactly this corpus, so a baseline recorded under one revision and a candidate measured under another are comparable. The corpus is described rather than listed: templates plus the pinned generator expand to the same bytes on every host, and corpusDigest is what proves it — a template edit that changed the corpus without changing this file's version would otherwise silently invalidate every recorded baseline.

corpus.$comment: Sized to fill the per-section rendered ceilings rather than sit sparsely under them. A corpus that fit comfortably would measure the cheap case and gate nothing.
corpus.$campaignProposedComment: Zero, and stated rather than quietly omitted. The Proposed lane is authored only by an agent tool call, whose invocation capability cannot be constructed outside a live turn without rebuilding several of its capability objects here — and a benchmark seeded through rebuilt scaffolding measures the scaffolding. Confirmed-lane cost is what a turn pays on every dispatch; Proposed-lane admission pressure is measured by CovenantContextPressureTests and is not gated here.

measurement.$comment: Warmup exists to retire first-call costs the shipped binary pays once per process, never to reach a state the product does not run in. Batches are the pairing unit for the comparative bootstrap, so a batch has to be long enough to be a stable observation and short enough that a run holds many of them.

$orderComment: Operations are measured in the order declared here, and the order is part of the workload. mutation.commit appends a real version on every iteration, so it leaves the corpus with more versions than it found — the heads it measures are unchanged, which is why the census below it is unaffected, but reordering these entries would still change what the ones after it measure. The corpus digest is taken at seed time and would not catch that.
$measurementBoundaryComment: What these operations do not cover, stated because every smaller exclusion here is stated. A live provider attempt pays two Covenant-only costs beyond planning and admission: it freezes a per-call envelope whose digest walks every message and every content part, so that cost scales with the whole transcript rather than with the Covenant corpus and is paid again on every attempt of the fallback loop; and it commits one disclosure row through a process-wide serialized writer, in an immediate transaction the ordering contract requires to complete before the bytes leave. Neither is measured, and narrowing the claim was chosen over extending the workload: the freezer and the real token estimator live in the Api project, which this host does not reference, and adding an operation changes the manifest digest and invalidates every baseline recorded before it. So no number below is the total per-turn cost of the Covenant, and turn.plan does not claim to be.
$ceilingsComment: Latency ceilings are derived rather than asserted. Each is ten times what a quiet shared CI runner measured for that percentile, rounded up to two significant figures. The two runs it is derived from measured identical code on the macos-26 workspace-check lane on 2026-08-29: run 33262061371 was quiet and passed, run 32943342814 was contended and failed, and the second is what a busy host does to these numbers — status.census p95 moved from 61.2us to 214.7us, three and a half times, with no code change at all. The ceilings this replaces were four times what a developer machine measures, and a shared runner is about twice a developer machine before any contention begins — this machine measures status.census p95 at 32.4us against that quiet runner's 61.2us — so four times a developer machine was 1.6 times a quiet runner by the time the gate ran, and ordinary scheduling noise is larger than that. Ten times a quiet runner is the multiple that matches what the gate is for: it catches an order-of-magnitude regression and nothing smaller, and it clears every figure either run produced by at least a further factor of two. The tightest is status.census p99, 780us against the contended run's 381.0us; a runner more than twice as contended as the worst yet recorded would trip that one first. turn.admission is deliberately outside this rule and keeps the ceilings it already had. It is the one operation that does not drift with the host — p95 3.5us quiet against 3.7us contended — so it has no noise to absorb, and its tightness is load-bearing: reducing what one provider attempt's admission costs per call is queued work, and a ceiling ten times looser would leave that improvement invisible to the gate that should be proving it. What holding it costs is stated rather than hidden. Its p50 is under three microseconds, so a single scheduler preemption is its entire p99, and a shared runner has already recorded 119.7us there against this 30us ceiling (2026-08-26, tabulated with the rest of that run in scripts/benchmark-covenant.sh). That is a known way for this lane to go red without a regression, accepted here so the admission measurement keeps its resolution. Allocation ceilings are untouched and far tighter — allocations are deterministic and machine-independent, the two runs above differ by at most two per cent, and this machine reproduces two of their figures exactly — so their only headroom needs to absorb a code change, not a host. That asymmetry is deliberate: latency catches order-of-magnitude regressions and allocation catches the ordinary kind.

operations.$comment: The Covenant's planning cost on every live turn: one snapshot read and one link over the whole corpus. It is the planning half of what a turn pays, not the whole of it — see $measurementBoundaryComment for the dispatch-time work no operation here covers. Measurement boundary: the Confirmed lane only. campaignProposedEntriesPerCampaign is zero and the bed has no retire path, so the linker's Retired-tombstone filtering and its Proposed-lane work are outside this number and this ceiling does not bound them.

One provider attempt's admission over a reused plan. Pure and provider-independent, and re-run per fallback candidate, so its cost multiplies by the number of candidates a turn tries. Two measurement boundaries: the Confirmed lane only, as above, and no tokenizer — the host measures sections and fragments with a fixed four-bytes-per-token estimate, because the planner takes its measurement as a delegate precisely so it stays provider-independent and folding a real tokenizer's cost in here would gate the tokenizer.
The operator write path's measurement half. It scans dependent heads across every Campaign for a Global key, so it is the write-path cost that grows with the installation.
The durable half: one serializable transaction appending one immutable version and advancing one head.
What memory status reads. Grouped and content-free, so it should stay flat as the corpus grows; a regression here means the grouping stopped happening in SQL.

comparison.$comment: Both conditions have to hold before a comparison blocks a merge: a single noisy run can push an observed ratio past the threshold on its own, so the bootstrap interval's lower bound has to clear its own bar too. These mirror BenchmarkRatioInterval.IsRegression and are restated here so a reader of the manifest can see the rule without reading the code.
